title: PRD: Hosted API overload protection (circuit breakers + load shedding)
creator: Nikhil Sharma
project: Reliability Program: Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding
description:
Owner: Nikhil Sharma (PM, Hosted API)
Partner PM: Lauren Bishop (Dedicated tier)
Eng leads: Ethan Park (Gateway/Control Plane), Mina Haddad (Smart Routing), Sofia Ivanova (Runtime Scheduling)
SRE leads: Rafael Mendes (program), Aisha Bello (dashboards/alerts)
Docs/Support: Elliot Price (Docs lead), Dev Patel (Support readiness)

Context
The Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable workloads (prompt length variance, streaming, tenant spikes, regional capacity dips). When overloaded, the current failure mode trends toward ambiguous timeouts and elevated 5xx, with noisy-neighbor effects and inconsistent retry behavior. This PRD defines the customer experience, tier policies, and rollout communications required for introducing explicit overload protection (circuit breakers + load shedding) in the Hosted request path.

Problem statement
When capacity or downstream dependencies are saturated, the platform currently degrades in ways that are:
- Hard for customers to interpret (timeouts vs 5xx, inconsistent messaging)
- Hard for customers to recover from safely (retry storms, no stable Retry-After semantics)
- Hard for Redwood to operate (tail-latency cascades, noisy neighbor amplification, unclear responsibility boundaries between gateway/routing/runtime)

We need predictable, well-instrumented overload behavior that protects global SLOs while giving customers stable, actionable responses.

Goals (customer-facing)
1) Predictable overload responses
- Customers receive explicit overload responses with stable HTTP status mapping, a stable error code, correlation/request IDs, and retry guidance.
- Overload failures should be distinguishable from internal server faults.

2) Prevent retry storms
- Responses must include consistent Retry-After semantics where applicable.
- Guidance must be clear enough that common client libraries/SDKs can implement safe exponential backoff with jitter.

3) Tenant- and tier-aware fairness
- Policies should prevent a single tenant or route from consuming disproportionate capacity.
- Enterprise tiers should get more stable throughput/latency behavior than self-serve, within what is contractually defined.

4) Safe degradation modes (opt-in / controlled)
- When configured, traffic may be routed to compatible fallback model variants or alternative regions.
- Under duress, non-essential features can be reduced (e.g., caps/limits) to preserve availability and avoid timeouts.

5) Operational transparency
- Customers should receive clear documentation (error codes + recommended retry) and predictable comms during canary/GA.
- Support should have playbooks and visibility to confirm whether a customer is being shed and why.

Non-goals (initial release)
- No changes to billing/credits policies beyond ensuring overload decisions are independent of billing enforcement.
- No major SDK surface redesign; only additive error handling improvements and example snippets.
- No commitment to cross-cloud capacity brokering beyond existing regional failover primitives.

Personas
1) Self-serve developers (PLG)
- Needs: simple semantics (429 vs 503), easy-to-follow retry guidance, minimal surprise.
- Risks: naive retries, tight loops, treating all 5xx as retryable.

2) Enterprise Hosted customers
- Needs: clear SLA/behavior expectations, predictable degradation, ability to tune caps, auditability (correlation IDs, consistent errors).

3) Dedicated customers (related)
- Not the primary target, but policy and messaging must not conflict with Dedicated SLAs or capacity guarantees. Dedicated should be insulated from Hosted noisy-neighbor dynamics.

User stories
- As a developer, when my request cannot be served due to overload, I receive a machine-readable error code and a Retry-After value so I can back off.
- As a platform team, I can distinguish overload shedding from internal 5xx to inform incident response and customer comms.
- As an enterprise customer, I can configure (or request) fallback behavior and understand the impact on latency/cost/quality.
- As Support/CS, I can use correlation IDs and dashboards to answer: “was this overload?”, “which policy triggered?”, and “what should the customer do next?”

Customer experience requirements
A) Error taxonomy + payload
- Must align with: Confluence ADR-014 (Hosted overload error taxonomy).
- Payload requirements (additive to existing JSON errors):
  - stable error code (e.g., OVERLOADED, RATE_LIMITED, DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE — final names per ADR)
  - message: customer-friendly, short, consistent
  - request_id / correlation_id (single canonical field name across gateway + downstream)
  - retry_after_ms or headers (Retry-After; exact contract per ADR)
  - optional details (safe, non-sensitive; avoid leaking internal capacity signals)
- HTTP status mapping principles:
  - Use 429 when the customer is being limited by an explicit quota/limit policy or fairness controls (tenant/route concurrency caps).
  - Use 503 when the system is overloaded or a dependency is unavailable and serving would risk cascade.
  - Avoid ambiguous 500 for overload paths.
- Backwards compatibility: responses remain JSON-compatible and additive. Do not remove existing fields.

B) Retry guidance contract
- Document and implement consistent behavior:
  - Clients should respect Retry-After.
  - Recommend exponential backoff with jitter.
  - Streaming: clarify whether to retry when partial tokens were streamed (generally: do not auto-retry non-idempotent operations; recommend idempotency keys where applicable).
  - Clarify which errors are safe to retry vs not.

C) Correlation IDs
- Every overload response must include a correlation/request ID that:
  - Customers can paste to Support
  - Support can use to query internal traces/logs
  - Does not encode sensitive info

D) Graceful degradation modes (product definition)
Controlled by policy flags. The allowed modes for the initial launch (to be finalized in PM-1191) include:
1) Fallback routing (opt-in)
- When enabled for a tenant/route/model:
  - fallback to a compatible model variant (e.g., same family, smaller size, quantized profile) or alternative region
  - bounded attempts (avoid loops)
  - preserve request semantics as much as possible (structured output/tool calling constraints must be explicit)
- Customer-facing considerations:
  - Must document that output may differ in quality/latency/cost when fallback is used.
  - Provide a response field/header indicating fallback was used (name TBD; must be safe and not expose internal topology).

2) Feature reduction under duress (opt-in, tier-aware)
- Examples (policy-defined, can be enabled by tenant or tier):
  - reduce max_tokens cap
  - limit streaming concurrency
  - limit tool-calling complexity (e.g., max tool calls or disable tools temporarily for certain tiers)
- Customer-facing requirements:
  - Must return explicit error or explicit applied-cap behavior (avoid silently changing semantics without visibility).
  - Documentation must list which knobs may be applied and how to detect them.

Tier policy (Hosted)
Objective: preserve global availability and fairness while offering tier-appropriate behavior.

Tiers in scope (Hosted API)
- Self-serve (default)
  - Stronger fairness controls; more aggressive shedding to protect p99 latency and prevent platform-wide impact.
  - Fallback routing: available as opt-in for eligible models/routes.
- Enterprise Hosted
  - Higher default limits and preferential admission within guardrails.
  - Better observability/support experience (faster escalation path; clearer comms).
  - Optional per-tenant policy overrides with review/guardrails.
- Dedicated
  - Not governed by Hosted shedding policies for normal operation; Dedicated capacity should remain isolated.
  - If shared control plane components shed, ensure messaging does not imply Dedicated capacity failure; clarify control-plane vs inference-plane behavior.

Policy principles
- Tenant isolation: a tenant’s burst should not dominate shared resources.
- Route/model specificity: policies can differ across endpoints (chat, embeddings) and across models.
- Regional independence: policies can be tuned per region based on capacity.
- Fail-safe defaults: conservative defaults that protect platform stability; explicit overrides require validation.

SLA / SLO considerations
- Must align with: Hosted API SLO update (overload exceptions and budget policy) and SLO toolkit classification updates.
- Product stance:
  - Overload shedding is a form of “graceful denial” to preserve overall availability and latency; however, customer-facing metrics should be transparent.
  - We should not classify overload as “success”; it is an error response that should be measurable and attributable.
  - Availability reporting: define whether overload errors count toward availability for each tier (to be finalized with SRE; document clearly).

Customer-facing commitments to define
- For each tier, define:
  - expected behavior under overload (429 vs 503 semantics)
  - typical Retry-After ranges (if we can safely characterize)
  - support escalation path and expected response times
  - whether fallback behavior is available and how it is indicated

Functional requirements (MVP)
- Standardized overload errors across gateway and relevant downstream services.
- Retry-After consistently set for overload responses when a retry is advisable.
- Clear separation between:
  - customer rate limiting/quota enforcement
  - overload shedding due to platform saturation
  - dependency health shedding (e.g., downstream store degraded)
- Tenant/tier aware policy evaluation (default tiers + per-tenant override capability with guardrails).
- Rollout controls: dark launch metrics, canary by region, progressive tenant enablement, fast rollback.

Observability and support readiness requirements
- Support-facing guidance: known issues doc explaining new overload errors, what customers should do, and how Support should triage.
- Internal dashboards:
  - shed rate, breaker open rate, queue depth/saturation indicators
  - breakdown by region/model/route/tier (bounded cardinality)
- Alerts:
  - triggers on sudden shed spikes, breaker oscillation, missing Retry-After regressions
- Runbooks:
  - oncall runbook for breaker incidents (verification, safe toggles, rollback)
- Instrumentation must allow answering:
  - “Is this overload or internal error?”
  - “Which policy triggered?”
  - “Is fallback working?”

Rollout and communication plan
Phases
0) Requirements + taxonomy alignment
- Confirm ADR-014 and customer-facing wording.
- Confirm SLA/SLO classification and reporting stance.

1) Dark launch (no customer behavior change)
- Emit overload decision metrics without enforcing.
- Validate cardinality, dashboards, and alert thresholds.

2) Canary (region + tenant subset)
- Start with one region (suggest us-east) and a small tenant cohort.
- Gate expansion on:
  - reduced timeouts/p99 during bursts
  - no significant increase in “false positive” shedding
  - Retry-After correctness and SDK compatibility

3) Progressive enablement to GA
- Expand by region and tier.
- Publish docs update and changelog.
- Support enablement complete prior to broad rollout.

Customer comms requirements
- Prior to canary (enterprise):
  - Heads-up email to impacted enterprise Hosted tenants in canary region(s) with:
    - what’s changing (explicit 429/503 semantics; Retry-After)
    - recommended client behavior
    - how to contact Support
- GA announcement:
  - Docs: “Handling overload errors” page + examples.
  - Changelog entry: new overload errors and retry contract.
  - Status page language template for overload events (avoid implying outage if shedding is operating as designed; coordinate with SRE).

Documentation deliverables
- Developer docs:
  - error codes + meanings
  - example responses (429/503)
  - retry guidance and sample code (Python/TS)
  - notes on streaming/idempotency
- Support docs:
  - escalation checklist
  - how to use correlation IDs
  - when to ask for tenant policy review

Open questions
- Final mapping of error codes to HTTP statuses and canonical field names (blocked on final ADR-014 text).
- Should we expose a “fallback_applied” indicator in response headers vs JSON? (Trade-off: visibility vs caching/compat risk.)
- For enterprise Hosted, do we offer customer-configurable policy knobs self-serve, or via Support-requested overrides only?
- What’s the official stance on whether overload errors count toward availability for each tier (Hosted self-serve vs enterprise Hosted)?
- Streaming retry behavior: do we recommend idempotency keys for chat/completions, and do we need a short-term SDK helper?

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Retry storms if Retry-After is missing/inconsistent
  - Mitigation: explicit automated tests; alert on missing Retry-After for overload codes; SDK examples.
- Risk: Customer confusion (“Is this an outage?”)
  - Mitigation: clear docs + support macros + status page wording; consistent error codes.
- Risk: False positives (over-shedding) harms customer success
  - Mitigation: dark launch, canary, tuning sheets per region/model; allow rapid rollback.
- Risk: Noisy neighbor persists due to insufficient tenant-aware controls
  - Mitigation: enforce concurrency/token bucket policies at gateway; coordinate with routing/runtime signals.

Success metrics
- Reduced p95/p99 latency under bursts compared to baseline.
- Fewer saturation-related incidents and lower severity.
- Reduced ambiguous timeouts and generic 5xx; increased share of explicit overload errors with stable semantics.
- Improved SLO error budget behavior during burst tests and real traffic.
- Support outcomes: reduced time-to-triage for overload-related tickets; fewer back-and-forths due to missing correlation IDs.

Latest updates
- 2025-11-07: Aligned with SRE on framing: explicit overload responses preferred over timeouts/5xx; need consistent Retry-After to prevent retry storms.
- 2025-11-12: Drafted tier policy principles; flagged open question on enterprise override process (self-serve vs ticketed).
- 2025-11-18: Added comms requirements for enterprise canary + GA changelog; waiting on final ADR-014 naming.

Acceptance criteria (for PM sign-off)
- Error semantics and payload finalized and documented (aligned with ADR-014).
- Tier policy written and reviewed with SRE + Control Plane + Routing leads.
- Comms plan includes enterprise canary outreach, GA docs/changelog, and support enablement checklist.
- Clear statement of SLA/SLO reporting stance for overload errors (by tier) agreed with SRE and documented.
